title: How to Get Bigger by Doing Less (The 85% Rule)
summary: NH lays out his '85% Rule', the framework behind all his programs: average effort sits around 85% of max, rep ranges stay roughly 6-12 (3-20 extremes), and progression runs through step loading, building reps and sets before a small weight jump. Frequency is treated as a recovery schedule matched to the workload, which he says makes deloads unnecessary.
claims: Minimalism saves time and energy but costs results; some accept ~80% of gains for half the work, NH prefers a maximized approach
Maximalist programs can also fail: so many exercises, sets and reps that intensity is sacrificed, which hurts as much as doing too little
The 85% Rule aims to do 'just enough': cut superfluous work and keep only quality sets and reps
The name comes from Dan Go's 85% rule for general athletics; NH applies the same mindset to hypertrophy
NH wants to stop the pendulum halfway, between the minimalism he pushed back against and excessive maximalism
85% is not a target for every set; it represents the average intensity across training, and this average dictates fatigue, frequency, sets, reps and volume
You train close to failure not to reach failure but to collect the high-quality reps just before it; the failure rep itself is not that special
1-3 rep sets are counter-indicated for hypertrophy because they bring 100% intensity with almost no volume
Rep ability at a given percentage of 1RM is individual: some can only do 2 reps at 90%, others 4; online percentage/RPE calculators mislead
A bodybuilder should skew strength toward rep strength rather than 1RM strength; a 10RM correlates more with muscle mass, a 1RM more with nervous system
Most people training for looks should use 6-12 reps, never going below 3-4 or above 15-20, which keeps intensity in the productive 60-90% zone
Intensity can swing (95% one day, 65% the next) as long as the bulk of the work averages around 85%; sticking to exactly 85% defeats the purpose
Intensity rises through a set: 8 squat reps starting at 75% climb rep by rep until the last one hits ~100% at failure
Stopping at about 90-95% rather than at 100% can be the better idea, but you must not stop so far from failure that the work becomes irrelevant
Sets above 15-20 reps rarely get close to failure because each added rep raises intensity less and less
The rule gives a 'strike zone': you know immediately if you have entered an irrelevant rep range through too much or too little intensity or volume
Volume and load must progress together: more reps and sets earn more weight on the bar, and if one stalls the other tends to stall too
Progression cycle: build reps and sets until a load that felt like 85% effort feels like 70%, then add weight to get back to 85%, cut back reps/sets and rebuild
Never just keep adding sets and reps at the same weight once effort has dropped to ~70%; that piles up volume without intensity and stops producing gains
Pushing toward 95% by cutting more volume would favor strength over volume accumulation, which is wrong for bodybuilding
Add volume conservatively: first reps (evolving rep range), then sets (same day or another day), then weight; this is step loading, always in small increments
Step-loading example: close-grip bench at 200 lb for 7, 6, 5 reps; build until the first set hits 10 and the last still gets 6 even with a fourth set added, then add weight
Unlike strength/hypertrophy block mesocycles, the 85% rule keeps fluctuations in volume and intensity small, because big intensity jumps always come at the expense of volume
Because fatigue never dips massively, the 85% rule makes deloads unnecessary
Linear periodization eventually fails: you cannot keep repeating last week's reps and sets with more weight, which leads to '5x5 syndrome' of plateaus, regression and frustration
5x5 works, but for bodybuilding there is no reason to prefer it over a flexible scheme like the 85% rule
Step loading guarantees you hit the next load because you have built enough volume at the previous one; better one step forward than three forward and two back
Conservative steps remove all-or-nothing anxiety: a miss costs one rep and almost never forces you to deload and drop weight
If you did 10, 9, 8, 8 at 200 lb on close-grip bench, a small jump will logically still give 7, 6, 6
The 85% rule deliberately does not maximize strength gains, since that would minimize volume accumulation
Go up in weight only when the load stops challenging you and has dipped to ~70% perceived effort; the goal is getting back to 85%, not getting stronger
Two lifters can reach a 250 lb bench at different speeds; the one who progressed through volume will be bigger at the same strength level
Volume is the variable most correlated with workload: adding a 10-rep set at 200 lb adds 2000 lb of tonnage, while adding 5 lb to a 10-rep set adds 50 lb
The recovery schedule must be planned, not guessed: if a session leaves you unable to train for longer than expected, that is poor planning
Frequency should be treated as a recovery schedule; there is no universally optimal frequency, only one that matches the work done to the recovery time allocated
If you train lats hard Monday and cannot match the volume Tuesday, you should have rested longer; if a 65%-effort Monday leaves 5 days of rest, the next session should move to Tuesday or Wednesday
The 85% rule is neither a shrinking nor an expanding rule but a management rule; NH rejects a fixed optimal number like hitting a muscle every 48 hours
Optimal-programming math fails in the gym because recovery fluctuates; aim for a flexible approach where the values simply match
Going to 99% effort is fine as long as it is not too often; otherwise recovery periods lengthen and frequency collapses
Once a week (HIT) can be made to fit the rule, but honest application pushes most people toward more balanced frequencies
Someone training 3x/week at 100% may do better 5x/week at 85%; someone training 6x/week at 70% may do better 4x/week at 90%
NH balances programs like a budget; every program he writes or critiques follows the 85% rule
Avoid rep ranges that redline the body and require long breaks, and avoid adding sets with irrelevant weights
Sign of doing too much: performance drops, meaning you lose reps and sets; for a bodybuilder the bar weight should never go backward, only volume dips temporarily after a load increase
Missing a rep target at the same weight (e.g. getting 7 instead of 8-9) is a milder warning that the muscle is under-recovered
Under-training shows up as lost volume capacity rather than lost strength; strength may even rise after a break, which is why people like deloads
A week of no volume (a deload) cannot be justified in bodybuilding even if the weight goes up afterward
Staying near 85% puts you in a flow state between anxiety (overtraining) and boredom (undertraining)
NH contrasts a Western 'no pain no gain' school, which builds fortitude but burns out longevity, with an Eastern 'flow' school of patience and autoregulation
Choose sets and load by what the body needs that day to be stimulated, not an arbitrary number or what you feel like lifting
Three sets of deadlifts to failure redline the body far more than three sets of curls to failure; intensity scales with the lift and the muscle mass involved
Five hard sets of deadlifts to failure can stop you from hinging heavy for at least a week; that fatigue is not justified and should be cut
Four heavy curl sets to failure are fine because only the biceps work, so you can train them again within about 3 days
Small muscles recover faster because they interact less with other muscles; the more interaction, the stricter the 85% rule must be applied
Failure on curls or lateral raises is fine if it does not stop you training them again soon; failure on squats that blocks leg training for a week is not
Failure is not needed for growth; proximity to failure is the point
Your 85% today is not your 85% tomorrow; the framework grows with you
exercises: step-load: add reps then a set, then a small weight jump
large systemic fatigue, can block hinging for a week
isolated muscle, low total fatigue, recovers in ~3 days
